newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says "flexible" on mining proposals.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says "flexible" on mining proposals.

text.p: Indonesia said on Tuesday it was willing to be flexible on controversial proposed amendments to its mining regulations after receiving responses from mining companies.
"There were various (counter) proposals, and the impact has to be seen from a wider perspective," Adjat Sudradjat, the director-general of mining, told reporters.
"We can discuss further. Our proposals are not final," he said.
Sudjarat said a number of mining companies had responded by the Tuesday deadline to the amendments, which are crucial for mining firms to carry out exploration and mining activities in the country.
"Many companies have responded. Some wanted changes, but the response is positive to settling (the issue)," he said. He gave no details.
Industry sources said the counter-proposals touched on official plans to allocate a 10 percent stake in future mining ventures to the government for free.
They also dealt with government proposals for mining companies with operations inside Indonesia to share capital gains made on stock exchanges outside the country with their shareholders.
Some mining analysts said the capital gains proposal would be virtually unenforceable.
Another contentious proposal ensures that capital increases made through a public share offering take place in Indonesia.

Mining and economic analysts said the proposed regulations, put forward last week, placed foreign investment in Indonesia in jeopardy -- and the country lacks capital to finance large-scale exploration work on its own.
The ministry summoned mining companies last Tuesday and told them the new rules were non-negotiable, but had softened its position by Thursday.
On Monday, there were questions as to whether the proposals would be enforced at all.
"They have not come to me yet," Mines and Energy Minister Ida Bagus Sudjana told reporters on Monday. Well-informed government sources said the proposals had come from the top levels of the ministry.
Mining sources said some of the amendments were acceptable, such as independent confirmation of ore reserves prompted by the Busang gold scandal.

Canadian mining company Bre-X Minerals Ltd had claimed to have made the biggest gold find of the century on Borneo island until an independent auditor earlier this year described it as the biggest mining fraud in history.
